question: Which of the following best distinguishes fever (pyrexia) from hyperthermia?

answers.text: Fever is always higher in magnitude than hyperthermia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Magnitude does not distinguish the two. Both can reach dangerous levels above 41°C.

answers.text: In fever the hypothalamic set-point is elevated, whereas in hyperthermia core temperature rises above a normal set-point

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Fever is a controlled thermostat reset by endogenous pyrogens; hyperthermia results from failure of heat dissipation with a normal set-point.

answers.text: Hyperthermia responds to antipyretics such as paracetamol, but fever does not

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The opposite is true. Antipyretics lower the hypothalamic set-point, so they work in fever but NOT in hyperthermia, which is why this distinction has direct therapeutic importance.

answers.text: Fever is caused exclusively by bacterial infections, while hyperthermia has non-infectious causes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fever has many non-infectious causes (autoimmune, malignant, drug-induced). Aetiology does not define the distinction.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the pathophysiology: fever = elevated set-point driven by IL-1β/IL-6/TNF-α → PGE₂; hyperthermia = set-point normal but heat balance overwhelmed.
Well done. Recognising that antipyretics work in fever but not hyperthermia is the single most clinically important consequence of this distinction.
